summary: Different locations on Earth have different environmental conditions, but there are no sites that perfectly match the Moon or Mars, this reduces the effectiveness of testing of equipment and missions on Earth. Terrestrial Analog Explorer addresses this by scoring Earth locations against both worlds using measured NASA data — temperature, elevation, and terrain ruggedness, with other additional factors. The website checks, ranks, and identifies the most suitable analog sites, and it has a built-in AI assistant that adds plain-language analysis and search to help users find the right location for testing specific equipment or rehearsing space missions.
details:
How does our website work?

The Terrestrial Analog Explorer begins by showing the target environments on Mars and Moon, that the analogs try to reproduce. This includes multiple factors such as mean temperature, dryness, regolith etc.

This is followed by explanation of each factor that the analog is looking for that matches the target environment. Additionally, famous terrestrial analogs that are used for testing and research are also displayed. The famous terrestrial analogs have also been ranked with NASA measured data to see its compatibility with Moon and Mars condition.

Using the measured NASA data — NASA POWER climatology (temperature, precipitation) and SRTM elevation. Earth locations are ranked and the top 8 Moon and Mars Analog are displayed, this includes famous terrestrial analogs, as well as discovering new sites that suit certain conditions. The top 8 analogs can change depending on the purpose of the mission.

The 3D globe works together with Google Gemini AI 2.5, which allows user to search for suitable analog sites, by typing in keywords such as the conditions of the location, or the purpose of testing and research mission. Users can click anywhere on the globe, and the website will pull location's real NASA environment data. The conditions are compared against the Moon and Mars, and a compatibility score between 0~100% is given. The result will display two scores (one for Moon, one for Mars). There will also be a summary of what the location matches or doesn't match, possible research and testing opportunities. A chart will also be provided that compares every factor.

A save function is also available for users to save the location(s) they have found.

Benefit:

  • Based on real NASA data → Scoring is measured using NASA climate and elevation data, which makes the result more trustworthy for planning
  • Flexibility → Different missions have different condition to meet and satisfy, some may need extremely hot conditions, while others may be low and dry terrain. Users can adjust what factors matter the most, or adjust the basis on what the rank should compared to, so the recommended sites will be adjusted to fit the specific purpose of each mission
  • Discovers new possibilities → This tool can locate lesser-known locations that match the Moon or Mars condition, opening new options for research and testing
  • Increasing accessibility → Interactive globe, with clear scores and explanations allow the public to understand why certain places on Earth can match and stand in for other planets

Intended Impact:

Discover lesser-known sites that can aid in early planning of Moon and Mars mission, as well as suggesting possible testing and research opportunities through data-driven results.

Additional Impact:

This website is open to everyone, allowing educational purposes for curious learners, such as learning about Moon and Mars conditions etc.

What makes this project creative?

  • Adaptability → User-adjustable conditions that allow ranking to be changed and re-sorted out to find most suitable analog sites for the intended testing purposes
  • Easy to understand → Terrestrial analogs can be quite complicated and require people to read multiple papers to understand the type of conditions that are compatible with Moon and Mars. This website summaries what conditions are needed without user spending time on reading papers. In addition, users find any location on Earth and compare to see how Moon/Mars like it is.
  • Scoring every location → This tool scores every point on Earth, not just famous terrestrial analog sites. This tool can evaluate any location on the planet, allowing discovery of lesser-known places that match Moon or Mars conditions.

Factors considered:

Measured (Directly from NASA data):

  1. Mean temperature → Affects material performances
  2. Temperature extremes → Day/Night swings mimic Moon's airless environment
  3. Aridity (dryness) → Dry ground is suitable for Mars analog
  4. Elevation / thin air → High altitude and thin air can mirror Mars atmospheric condition
  5. Terrain ruggedness → Rugged, steep or cratered ground mirrors the Moon and Martian terrain
  6. Illumination regime → Lighting affects how much solar energy is received

Estimated (informed models, not direct measurements):

  1. Regolith / surface material → Abrasive, iron and volcanic soil can resemble lunar and Martian ground, needed for testing suits and rovers
  2. Geological features → Landforms such as impact craters mimic Moon and Mars feature, suitable for analog work
  3. Remoteness / isolation → Recreate the realism of outer space mission

Tools and Technology

  • Development tools → Kiro IDE (AI-powered editor, built on VS code), Python
  • Infrastructure and Technological Hosting → Netlify (Frontend), Google AI Studio (Gemini API), OpenTopoData (SRTM elevation API)
  • Frontend & UI → HTML5, CSS3, vanilla Javascript (no framework), responsive light/dark theming
  • 3D & Visualization → Globe.GL (3D Earth globe), Three.js (3D rendering engine), Leaflet (2D surface maps), Chart.js (factor comparison charts)
  • Programming Language → HTML, CSS, Python, Javascript
  • AI & Machine Learning → Google Gemini API 2.5(in-app natural-language analysis and search), measured-data scoring model built from NASA climate and elevation datasets
  • Software & Design → CSS and UI developed with AI assistance (Claude via Kiro) under team direction; No design tool and no AI-generated imagery were used
  • Hardware → Standard development and analysis computer
  • Data sources → NASA datasets (POWER, SRTM, GIBS, Trek, EONET), open-licensed imagery
